lessons.title: The Memory Model: Stack, Heap, and the GC
lessons.content:
# The Memory Model: Stack, Heap, and the GC

Performance work in .NET starts with one question: **what is this code allocating?**

## Where values live

```csharp
int x = 42;                      // stack slot inside the current frame
var point = new Point(1, 2);     // struct: inline, no heap allocation
var list = new List<int>();      // class: header + fields on the managed heap
```

- **Value types** (`int`, `struct`, `record struct`, enums) live inline: on the stack when they are locals, inside their owner when they are fields.
- **Reference types** (`class`, `record`, arrays, `string`, delegates) always live on the heap; the variable holds a reference.

Every heap object carries roughly 16 bytes of overhead on x64 (object header plus method table pointer) before your own fields.

## Generational garbage collection

The GC divides the heap into generations based on one observation: most objects die young.

| Generation | Contains | Collected |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Gen 0** | Freshly allocated objects | Very often, very cheap |
| **Gen 1** | Gen 0 survivors, a buffer | Less often |
| **Gen 2** | Long-lived objects | Rarely, expensive |
| **LOH** | Arrays/objects >= 85,000 bytes | With Gen 2, not compacted by default |

Allocation itself is a pointer bump, essentially free. The cost is **collection**, and collection cost scales with how many objects *survive*, not how many you allocated. A million short-lived objects that all die in Gen 0 are cheaper than a thousand that get promoted to Gen 2.

```csharp
Console.WriteLine(GC.GetTotalAllocatedBytes(precise: true));
Console.WriteLine($"gen0={GC.CollectionCount(0)} gen1={GC.CollectionCount(1)} gen2={GC.CollectionCount(2)}");
```

## The classic allocation traps

```csharp
// 1. String concatenation in a loop: one new string per iteration
string s = "";
foreach (var item in items) s += item + ",";           // O(n^2) copying

var sb = new StringBuilder();
foreach (var item in items) sb.Append(item).Append(',');   // one growing buffer

// 2. Boxing: a value type forced onto the heap
object boxed = 42;                                     // allocation
ArrayList old = new(); old.Add(42);                    // allocation per item
List<int> modern = new(); modern.Add(42);              // none, generics avoid boxing

// 3. Closures: the lambda captures state into a compiler-generated class
foreach (var id in ids)
    tasks.Add(Task.Run(() => Process(id)));            // one closure object per iteration

// 4. LINQ in a hot path: each operator allocates an enumerator and delegates
var count = items.Where(i => i.Active).Count();        // fine once, costly per frame
```

None of these are wrong. They are wrong *in a hot loop*, and the way you find out which loop is hot is measurement, not intuition.

## Structs and where they help

```csharp
public readonly record struct Vec2(float X, float Y)
{
    public float Length => MathF.Sqrt(X * X + Y * Y);
}

var points = new Vec2[1_000_000];   // one array allocation, zero per element
```

An array of structs is one contiguous block: no per-element object headers, no pointer chasing, and it plays well with the CPU cache. `readonly record struct` also stops defensive copies on property access.

> [!WARNING]
> Do not call `GC.Collect()` in production code. It forces a full blocking collection, discards the GC's tuning heuristics, and almost always makes throughput worse. The exception is a benchmark harness measuring a steady state.

lessons.title: Benchmarking and Profiling: Measure, Then Optimize
lessons.content:
# Benchmarking and Profiling: Measure, Then Optimize

A stopwatch around a loop in a Debug build measures the JIT warming up, not your code. Use the real tools.

## BenchmarkDotNet

```bash
dotnet new console -o Benchmarks
cd Benchmarks
dotnet add package BenchmarkDotNet
```

```csharp
using BenchmarkDotNet.Attributes;
using BenchmarkDotNet.Running;

[MemoryDiagnoser]                       // report allocations alongside time
public class ParseBenchmarks
{
    private readonly string _line = "2026-09-03,checkout,1299.00";

    [Benchmark(Baseline = true)]
    public decimal WithSplit() => decimal.Parse(_line.Split(',')[2]);

    [Benchmark]
    public decimal WithSpan()
    {
        ReadOnlySpan<char> s = _line;
        int last = s.LastIndexOf(',');
        return decimal.Parse(s[(last + 1)..]);
    }
}

BenchmarkRunner.Run<ParseBenchmarks>();
```

```bash
dotnet run -c Release      # Release, always: Debug numbers are meaningless
```

```
| Method    | Mean      | Ratio | Allocated |
|---------- |----------:|------:|----------:|
| WithSplit | 118.42 ns |  1.00 |     160 B |
| WithSpan  |  47.10 ns |  0.40 |         - |
```

BenchmarkDotNet handles the parts everyone gets wrong by hand: warmup iterations, JIT tiering, multiple processes, outlier removal, and statistical significance. `[MemoryDiagnoser]` adds the allocation column, which is often the number that matters most.

## Reading the numbers honestly

- **Ratio beats absolute time.** Nanoseconds vary by machine; a 0.40 ratio does not.
- **Allocated bytes predict GC pressure**, which is throughput at scale even when per-call time looks fine.
- **Watch the error/StdDev columns.** A 5% improvement inside a 10% error bar is noise.
- **Benchmark a realistic input.** Sorting 10 elements says nothing about sorting 10 million.

## Profiling a whole application

```bash
dotnet tool install --global dotnet-counters
dotnet tool install --global dotnet-trace
dotnet tool install --global dotnet-dump

dotnet-counters monitor --process-id 1234 --counters System.Runtime
dotnet-trace collect --process-id 1234        # open the .nettrace in PerfView or VS
dotnet-dump collect --process-id 1234         # then: dotnet-dump analyze, dumpheap -stat
```

`dotnet-counters` is the first stop for a live service: allocation rate, Gen 0/1/2 counts, thread-pool queue length, exception rate, and working set, with no restart and almost no overhead.

## A working order of operations

1. Reproduce the problem with a **measurement**, not a hunch.
2. Profile to find where the time or allocation actually goes.
3. Fix the single largest contributor.
4. Re-measure. Keep the change only if the number moved.
5. Add a benchmark to the repo so a future refactor cannot silently undo it.

> [!WARNING]
> The most common false result in .NET benchmarking is a dead-code elimination: if a benchmark method's result is never used, the JIT can delete the work entirely and report an impossible 0.3 ns. Always return the value from the method, which is exactly what BenchmarkDotNet consumes for you.

lessons.title: Final Project: Optimize and Harden a .NET Service
lessons.content:
# Final Project: Optimize and Harden a .NET Service

Take a service that works and make it fast, observable, and safe. Start from your Intermediate task API or write a small ingestion service, either is fine, as long as it processes a data file and exposes an HTTP API.

## Requirements

1. **Establish a baseline.** Generate a CSV of at least 500,000 rows. Write a naive parser using `File.ReadAllLines` plus `Split`, and benchmark it with BenchmarkDotNet under `[MemoryDiagnoser]`. Record time and allocated bytes; this is the number you must beat.
2. **Optimize the hot path.** Rewrite the parser using `File.ReadLines` (or a `StreamReader`), `ReadOnlySpan<char>` slicing, span-based `TryParse` overloads, and `ArrayPool<byte>` or `stackalloc` where a buffer is needed. Target at least a 2x time improvement and a 90% reduction in allocations, and show the before/after benchmark table in your README.
3. **Prove it in the process, not just the microbenchmark.** Run the service under load and capture `dotnet-counters` output for allocation rate and Gen 0/1/2 collection counts, before and after. Explain any result that contradicts the benchmark.
4. **Layer the codebase.** Split into `Domain`, `Application`, `Infrastructure`, and `Api` projects with references pointing inward only. The domain project must have no dependency on EF Core, ASP.NET Core, or your parser's IO.
5. **Make it resilient.** Every outbound HTTP call goes through `IHttpClientFactory` with timeout, retry, and circuit breaker. Add `/health/live` and `/health/ready` with the correct split, and a `BackgroundService` that honours its stopping token.
6. **Secure it.** JWT bearer authentication with full token validation, at least two named authorization policies (one claim-based, one resource-based), a CORS policy limited to a single origin, security headers, and no secret anywhere in `appsettings.json`.
7. **Make it observable.** OpenTelemetry tracing and metrics with an OTLP exporter, structured logging with a correlation id per request, and no secrets or PII in any log line.

## Stretch goals

- Add an outbox table so a crash between "save order" and "publish event" cannot lose the event, and prove it by killing the process mid-flight.
- Publish with `PublishTrimmed` or Native AOT and compare cold-start time and memory against the framework-dependent build.
- Add a `Server-Timing` header or a custom `Meter` that reports parse duration per request.
- Add a load test (k6, Bombardier, or NBomber) to CI and fail the build when p99 latency regresses beyond a threshold.

Submit a link to your finished repository, including the benchmark results and a short write-up of what you changed and why. An instructor will review it before you can mark this lesson complete.
